teaching.causalExplanation: Remember nuclide notation. The top number, the mass number, counts the protons and neutrons in the nucleus. Together, they're called nucleons. The bottom number, the atomic number, counts the protons, so it's also the charge on the nucleus. In a nuclear reaction, nucleons get rearranged, but none appear from nothing, and neither does charge. So the top numbers must add up to the same total on both sides, and so must the bottom numbers. To use this, every particle needs the same two numbers. An alpha particle is a helium nucleus, so it's written as helium, with four on top and two on the bottom. A beta particle is an electron. It isn't a nucleon, so its top number is zero, and its charge is minus one, so its bottom number is minus one. A gamma ray has neither, so it's zero and zero. And a neutron is one on top, and zero on the bottom, because it has no charge. Let's balance the uranium. On the left, uranium-two-thirty-eight has two hundred and thirty-eight on top, and ninety-two on the bottom. On the right, the alpha particle takes four and two. So the new nucleus must have two hundred and thirty-eight minus four on top, which is two hundred and thirty-four. And ninety-two minus two on the bottom, which is ninety. Now, which element has ninety protons? The periodic table says thorium. Check both rows. Two thirty-four plus four is two thirty-eight, and ninety plus two is ninety-two. It's balanced.

scenes.teachingReason: Now a reaction people make happen. In a nuclear reactor, cobalt-fifty-nine is hit with neutrons. When uranium-two-thirty-five absorbs a neutron, it splits into barium-one-forty-one and krypton-ninety-two, and three neutrons fly out. scenes.teachingReason: So what actually changes in each nucleus? Alpha decay removes two protons and two neutrons. Beta decay turns one neutron into a proton. Both change the number of protons, so both turn one element into another. That's called transmutation. Gamma changes no particles at all. And adding a neutron keeps the same element, but makes a heavier isotope.

scenes.teachingReason: Notice that nuclear reactions change the nucleus itself. Ordinary chemical reactions never do. They only move electrons. When a sodium atom loses one electron, it keeps its eleven protons, so it becomes a sodium ion, with a charge of plus one. A chlorine atom that gains one electron becomes a chloride ion, minus one. Next time, we'll use charges like these to work out the formula of a compound.
